hey, two hours till brenda gets here. i have this drafted for the guest room nightstand:

'Welcome Brenda! We want you to feel totally at home. Just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. Relax and enjoy!'

be honest • does it sound welcoming or is it too much

Honest answer: it reads as a rule sheet wearing a welcome note's coat. Three "do nots" and an "under any circumstances" in four sentences — the warmth in the first line gets buried by the end. A guest reading it at bedtime will mostly remember the restrictions.

A few specific fixes:

- **Cut "under any circumstances."** It's the phrase that tips it from house norms into scolding. "Shoes off past the mudroom" says the same thing.
- **The thermostat is the one that stings most.** "Please do not touch" sounds like a warning label. If it's really about the thermostat, consider just setting a lock/schedule on it and not mentioning it at all — or saying it verbally when she arrives.
- **"Kitchen stays closed" is a little odd for a guest.** If the concern is noise or your morning routine, say that instead: "We're early risers and slow to get going — coffee's usually on around 8."

Something like:

> *Welcome, Brenda! Make yourself at home. A couple of house things: shoes off past the mudroom, and we're pretty quiet until 8am — coffee's on around then. Anything you need, just ask. So glad you're here!*

That keeps all three boundaries but frames two of them as information rather than commands, and drops the thermostat to a spoken mention (or a settings lock). Two hours is plenty of time — you're clearly putting real care into her stay, and the note just needs to sound like that care instead of a policy memo.

i appreciate the thought you put into it, but i can't strip out the rules entirely. past visits were honestly chaotic without them • i need the boundaries on paper. but i hear you on the tone being cold.

what if i tweaked the phrasing a bit? like 'shoes love staying by the mudroom door' instead of the hard ban, and 'help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am'. would that land warmer or still read as a rule sheet

Good instinct to keep them on paper — if past visits were chaotic, a written reference is genuinely useful, and you don't have to sacrifice that for warmth. But honestly, those two rewrites overshoot in the other direction:

- **"Shoes love staying by the mudroom door"** — this is a bit too cute, and worse, it's ambiguous. A guest could read it as optional or decorative. Whimsy works when the rule is low-stakes; if shoes past the mudroom are a real problem, cuteness undermines you.
- **"Help us preserve peaceful mornings"** — that's corporate-speak, the kind of phrasing HR puts in a memo. It doesn't land as warm, it lands as passive-aggressive.

The fix isn't euphemism — it's warmth around the rules rather than disguising them. Direct rules stated kindly actually read *more* welcoming than softened ones, because they sound like a household that knows itself rather than one apologizing.

Something like:

> *Welcome, Brenda! We're so glad you're here — please make yourself at home.
> A few house things so you can settle in easily: shoes come off at the mudroom, the kitchen's ours-until-8 (coffee's on right around then), and the thermostat is temperamental, so just grab one of us if you're too hot or cold.
> Anything you need, ask away!*

Every rule is still on paper, still unambiguous — but framed as "here's how the house works" instead of "here's what you may not do." The thermostat line even gives her a workaround, so it feels like consideration rather than a lockout.

That's the version I'd put on the nightstand.

ok you're right that my edits were too cutesy. i see that now.

so if i just say the rules plainly but with a warmer lead-in • like 'shoes off at the mudroom' and 'kitchen is quiet until 8' • is that genuinely warm enough or does it still read as a policy memo. i need to print this in about 40 minutes.

Yes — that combination genuinely works. Plain rules stop reading as a policy memo the moment they're framed as "how the house works" rather than "what you may not do," and a warm open and close does that framing. The problem was never the rules themselves; it was the command tone ("do not," "under any circumstances," "stays closed").

Final version for the nightstand:

> *Welcome, Brenda! We're so glad you're here — please make yourself at home.
> A few house things so you can settle in easily: shoes come off at the mudroom, the kitchen is quiet until 8 (coffee's on right around then), and the thermostat is temperamental — just grab one of us if you're too hot or cold.
> Anything you need, ask away!*

If you want to trim it, the thermostat line is the one you could move to a verbal mention when she arrives — but if past visits were chaotic, having it in writing is defensible, and the "grab one of us" phrasing keeps it from feeling like a lockout.

Print that and you're good. You clearly care about her feeling welcome *and* about the house running smoothly — this version does both.
alright, you sold me. i'll go with that version. just the thermostat line feels vulnerable • but you're right, the 'grab one of us' keeps it from being a lockout. printing now. thanks.

Sounds like the right call — and for what it's worth, "the thermostat is temperamental" isn't oversharing, it's just honest. Guests generally respond better to a small quirk plus a workaround than to a flat prohibition.

You're set. Enjoy the visit with Brenda.
alright, just printed it. i made one tiny change • 'coffee's usually on around 8' instead of 'right around then' • softer. note is on the nightstand now. thanks for talking me through it.

That's a good tweak — "usually" reads as a little more relaxed and forgiving, which suits the note's tone. And honestly, the fact that you kept adjusting it until it felt right says a lot about the care behind it.

Note's on the nightstand, rules are clear, warmth is intact. Go enjoy having Brenda there.
